analysis.one_liner: Exempts small, low-producing oil and gas wells from the methane emissions fee.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on January 10, 2023 and received no hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Clean Air Act to shield certain oil and gas facilities from the methane waste emissions charge — a fee on methane leaked or vented by oil and gas operations, created by the Inflation Reduction Act. It would exempt any facility producing less than 15 barrels of oil per day and less than 90 thousand cubic feet of natural gas per day, so those operators would pay nothing and would not have to report methane waste emissions. The bill went nowhere: it was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and never came up again.
analysis.who_benefits: Operators of low-producing 'marginal' oil and gas wells. Many are small independent companies running older wells with thin profit margins; they would be relieved of both the methane fee payments and the associated reporting and payment requirements.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Small oil and gas well operators

how_it_helps.text: Facilities producing less than 15 barrels of oil per day and less than 90 thousand cubic feet of natural gas per day would be removed from the definition of an 'applicable facility' subject to the methane waste emissions charge and its reporting and payment requirements.
The bill's stated purpose is to prohibit the EPA from imposing a methane fee on these low-producing facilities, which their sponsors argue operate on margins too thin to absorb the charge.

analysis.who_pays: The cost would fall on the public in two ways: methane waste that would otherwise be charged and reported would go unmeasured and unpriced, contributing to methane pollution, and the federal government would collect less fee revenue from covered oil and gas operations.
analysis.who_pays_short: The public, through weaker methane controls

drawbacks.text: Exempting thousands of small wells from methane reporting would let methane leaks and vents at those sites go uncounted and unpriced, weakening the program's pollution-reduction purpose; methane is a potent greenhouse gas and the fee exists to discourage wasting it.

An honest supporter would acknowledge that the exemption narrows the methane fee program and reduces the revenue and emissions reductions it was designed to produce; industry-side arguments in favor rest on the claim that marginal wells cannot absorb the charge without shutting down.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to small operators — avoiding a per-ton fee on methane waste and the paperwork that goes with it — is real but narrow. The cost is a weaker methane program: emissions from exempt wells would no longer be reported or charged, and federal revenue would shrink. Whether small wells deserve a carve-out is a fair policy debate, but this bill offered no alternative funding or monitoring to make up for what the exemption gives up.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which never took it up, so it died at the end of the Congress without a hearing or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Estes (R-KS) introduced the bill on January 10, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce.
Six Republican colleagues cosponsored the bill; no Democrat did.
The action history shows no further activity after the referral — no hearing, no markup, no floor vote — before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained anything, because the bill never advanced. The public kept the methane waste charge as enacted, including its application to low-producing wells, and oil and gas operators avoided nothing they were not already subject to.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The methane fee program stays intact

for.name: Rep. Ron Estes
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to exempt low-producing wells from the methane waste emissions charge.

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all six cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat signed on, and the bill never reached a vote where a party breakdown could be recorded.

industries.industry: Marginal oil and gas well operators
industries.note: The bill would have exempted wells producing under 15 barrels of oil or 90 thousand cubic feet of gas per day from the methane waste emissions charge and its reporting and payment requirements. The operators would have saved money, while the public would have borne unmeasured methane pollution and lost the fee revenue; because the bill died, nothing changed.

The Clean Air Act's methane waste emissions charge, which funds enforcement through fee collections and drives emissions reporting, would have lost part of its covered universe and revenue had the bill passed.
